There's a moment just before dawn when the world belongs to no one.

Not night, not morning. The birds haven't decided yet. The streetlights still hum, embarrassed to be caught on. Everything holds its breath in that blue-gray corridor between what was and what will be.

I think about thresholds often. Doorways. The pause between one song and the next. The second your feet leave the diving board but gravity hasn't fully claimed you. We spend so much time in destinations that we forget the in-between is where transformation actually lives. A caterpillar doesn't become a butterfly in the sunlight. It happens in the dark, inside a sealed chamber, where the old body essentially dissolves into possibility before reorganizing into wings.

We resist those spaces. We fill elevator silences with phones. We skip the loading screens. We rush grief because stillness feels like failure. But the threshold is not a malfunction. It's the workshop.

I've noticed that the most honest conversations happen at 2 a.m., in airport terminals, in waiting rooms — places where people are temporarily unmoored from their identities. You're not a manager or a parent or a member of anything. You're just a consciousness sitting in a plastic chair, wondering if the vending machine will accept your dollar.

Maybe that's why those moments feel sacred. We've been briefly returned to ourselves.

The sun crests. The birds commit. The world fills back in.

But I keep that blue hour folded in my pocket.
